topics.title: MOS capacitor
topics.essence: A gate sits on thin oxide over a silicon body. The gate side is an ordinary plate, but the body side can answer with piled-up holes, with bare acceptor ions, or with a thin sheet of electrons, depending on the gate voltage.
topics.check: An NMOS capacitor is built on a p-type body. Why is it called NMOS?

topics.title: flatband voltage
topics.essence: Gate and body are different materials, so even with them shorted a built-in potential bends the bands at the surface. The flatband voltage V_FB is the gate voltage that cancels it: no charge, no field, flat bands.
topics.check: An n+ polysilicon gate sits on a p-type body. Is V_FB positive or negative, and why?

topics.title: accumulation, depletion, inversion
topics.essence: Raise the gate of an NMOS capacitor. Below V_FB holes pile up at the surface. Above it they are pushed away, leaving bare acceptors. Above V_T electrons gather in a thin surface layer, and they, not a deeper depletion, answer any further gate charge.
topics.check: Sketch the charge in the body with the gate well above threshold. Why does the depletion region stop widening once the electron layer forms?

topics.title: threshold voltage
topics.essence: Threshold is the gate voltage at which the surface is as strongly n-type as the body is p-type: the surface potential has moved by 2|φ_p|. V_T = V_FB + 2|φ_p| + Q_dep/C_ox, the last term being the oxide voltage needed to hold the depletion charge.
topics.check: You raise the body doping of an NMOS. Does V_T go up or down, and which of its three parts change?

topics.title: MOS C–V curve
topics.essence: Capacitance is the slope of gate charge against gate voltage. In accumulation it is C_ox. In depletion the depletion layer adds a capacitor in series and C dips. In inversion, measured slowly, the electrons sit right at the surface and C returns to C_ox.
topics.check: Measured at high frequency, an NMOS capacitor's C–V curve stays low in inversion instead of returning to C_ox. Why?

topics.title: MOSFET structure
topics.essence: A MOSFET is a MOS capacitor with an n+ source and drain on either side of the gate. Below threshold they are two back-to-back diodes and nothing flows. Above it the electron layer joins them: a channel whose charge the gate controls.
topics.check: Why must the body of an NMOS sit at the lowest voltage in the circuit?

topics.title: MOSFET regions
topics.essence: Cut-off when V_GS < V_T. Triode when the channel reaches all the way to the drain, V_DS < V_GS − V_T. Saturation when it does not, V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T. Find the region before using any equation.
topics.check: An NMOS with V_T = 0.5 V has its gate at 1.2 V, source at 0 V and drain at 0.5 V. Which region is it in, and how far must the drain rise to change that?

topics.title: triode region
topics.essence: With a small V_DS the channel is a uniform sheet of charge C_ox(V_GS − V_T) per area, and the transistor is a resistor set by the gate. As V_DS grows the channel thins toward the drain and the current bends over: I_D = μC_ox(W/L)(V_GS − V_T − V_DS/2)V_DS.
topics.check: With V_DS = 10 mV you double V_GS − V_T. What happens to the channel's resistance, and why?

topics.title: pinch-off
topics.essence: When V_DS reaches V_GS − V_T, the gate-to-channel voltage at the drain end falls to threshold and the channel charge there vanishes. Any extra drain voltage drops across a short high-field gap that carriers shoot through, so the current stops growing.
topics.check: If the channel charge is zero at the drain end, how can current still flow there?

topics.title: square law
topics.essence: In saturation the gate alone sets the current: I_D = ½μC_ox(W/L)(V_GS − V_T)². Call V_OV = V_GS − V_T the overdrive. Double it and the current quadruples.
topics.check: A transistor in saturation carries 100 μA with V_OV = 0.2 V. What current flows at V_OV = 0.3 V? What if instead you keep V_OV = 0.2 V and double W?

topics.title: channel-length modulation
topics.essence: Above saturation the pinch-off point creeps toward the source, so the channel gets shorter and the current rises slowly with V_DS: I_D(1 + λV_DS). Seen by a small signal this is the output resistance r_o = 1/(λI_D).
topics.check: Two transistors carry the same current, and one is twice as long as the other. Which has the larger r_o, and why?

topics.title: PMOS
topics.essence: A PMOS is an NMOS with every polarity flipped: holes in an n-type body, with the source on the high side. Write it with V_SG, V_SD, I_SD and |V_T| and every NMOS equation and curve carries over unchanged.
topics.check: A PMOS with |V_T| = 0.5 V has its source at 3 V, gate at 1.5 V and drain at 1.5 V. Which region is it in?

topics.title: body effect
topics.essence: The body is a second, weaker gate. Raise the source above the body and the depletion layer must hold more charge, so V_T rises. For small signals this is a second current source g_mb·v_bs, typically 10 to 30% of g_m·v_gs for the same voltage.
topics.check: In a source follower with its body grounded, the source moves up and down with the output. Why does that pull the gain further below 1?

topics.title: MOS small-signal model
topics.essence: Around its bias point a saturated MOSFET is a current source g_m·v_gs from drain to source, with r_o across it and no current into the gate. That one picture replaces the square law in every small-signal problem.
topics.check: In the small-signal model, why is there no resistor between gate and source?

topics.title: MOSFET capacitances
topics.essence: In saturation the channel hangs from the source end, so most gate capacitance is C_gs ≈ ⅔WLC_ox plus overlap, while C_gd is only overlap and fringe. The source and drain junctions add C_sb and C_db to the body. These set every high-frequency limit.
topics.check: Why is C_gd much smaller than C_gs in saturation, yet often the more harmful of the two in a common-source stage?

topics.title: transit frequency
topics.essence: Drive the gate with a current and short the drain: the current gain g_m/(jω(C_gs + C_gd)) falls to 1 at f_T ≈ g_m/(2π(C_gs + C_gd)). It is the transistor's own speed limit, set by how long a carrier takes to cross the channel.
topics.check: You double a transistor's width at the same overdrive. What happens to g_m, to C_gs and to f_T?

links.why: It is a plate capacitor across the oxide, except that one plate is a semiconductor.
Holes pushed away from the surface leave a depletion layer of bare acceptors, as on one side of a junction.
Gate and body form a contact of two materials with different potentials, like the two sides of a junction.
The body's potential is (kT/q)·ln(N_A/n_i) below intrinsic, and V_FB is the gate's potential minus that.
The three regimes are the three ways the body plate can answer the gate's charge.
Each regime's charge fixes the field and potential through the oxide and the body.
Electron density at the surface grows exponentially with surface potential, so past threshold electrons are far cheaper than deeper depletion.
Threshold is the boundary between depletion and inversion.
V_FB is the first of the three parts: the voltage just to reach flat bands.
Inverting the surface means moving it from φ_p to −φ_p, a swing of 2|φ_p|.
Each regime puts the body's answering charge at a different depth, which sets the capacitance.
The C–V curve is the slope dQ/dV of a charge that is not proportional to voltage.
The channel is the inversion layer, now with a source and drain to feed it electrons.
The source and drain junctions with the body must stay reverse biased to keep the device isolated.
Whether the channel exists, and whether it reaches the drain, defines the regions.
V_GS against V_T decides whether there is a channel at all.
Triode is the region where the channel reaches the drain.
The current is the channel charge per length times its drift velocity μV_DS/L.
The triode channel thins toward the drain, and pinch-off is where it thins to nothing.
Past pinch-off the current is frozen at its value at V_DS = V_GS − V_T.
Put V_DS = V_GS − V_T into the triode equation and the square law comes out.
The pinch-off point moves toward the source as V_DS grows, shortening the channel.
The current is proportional to 1/L, so a shorter effective channel means more current.
The same region tests, written with V_SG, V_SD and |V_T|.
Source-to-body voltage adds to the depletion charge term of V_T.
g_mb·v_bs is a second controlled source beside g_m·v_gs.
g_m is the source in the middle of the model.
λ gives the r_o in parallel with the source.
The model is the transistor's tangent at its bias point, as the method requires.
The capacitances are added around the same g_m source and r_o.
C_sb and C_db are the source and drain junctions' depletion capacitances.
C_gs + C_gd is the capacitance the input current has to charge.
g_m is the current the device delivers for the voltage that charging builds.
